title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was deployed to generate a fake interview article impersonating a real finance presenter and central bank governor in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fabricated content was designed to appear credible enough to deceive people into investing money. This represents a use of generative AI outside any legitimate deployment context, repurposed entirely as a tool for fraud.

The failure occurred at the point of deployment into the world without any human verification that the content was authentic or that it was authorized to use real people's likenesses and names. Catching this would have required either preventing the generation of impersonation content at the model level, or implementing a human review process before publishing. It is not established who built or operated the system that generated this content.

Investment scams using this method have increased sharply according to regulatory data. The sophistication and volume of AI-generated impersonation attempts means that systems designed to detect fraudulent content, and processes meant to verify the authenticity of financial endorsements, are not keeping pace with the speed at which this content can be produced.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a staged confrontation represents a growing type of investment scam. The fabricated interview promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, with the fictional story designed to appear credible. This type of AI-generated scam is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated in Australia.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data shows investment scams are rising sharply, with 19,400 schemes removed last year, a 182 percent increase. The regulator removed 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and wealthy businesspeople including Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. ASIC recommends consumers verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through its free public registers before investing and warns that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy.
